what_it_does: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) asks: given a list of cities, what is the shortest route that visits every city exactly once? It is famously hard for conventional computers as the number of cities grows. One hardware approach is an Ising solver — a chip that mimics a physical system of magnetic spins settling into their lowest-energy state, which corresponds to finding a near-optimal route. TAXI tackles large TSPs by first splitting the cities into smaller clusters (hierarchical clustering) and solving each cluster on a separate hardware unit (called a crossbar macro — a grid of memory cells that can do math in place), so the subproblems run in parallel without shuffling data between units. The random noise that helps these solvers explore different routes is generated by small magnetic memory devices called SOT-MRAMs (a type of non-volatile memory that can switch states using a spin current), which act as compact, energy-efficient random-number sources. The concern raised is that quality can degrade as problem size grows beyond a certain point with this clustering strategy.
